claim: The signalling cascade underlying moulting differs between Panarthropoda and the remaining ecdysozoans.
source: Despite superficial similarities, the signalling cascade underlying moulting differs between Panarthropoda and the remaining ecdysozoans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding of the study.

claim: Eclosion hormone (EH) and bursicon originated prior to the cnidarian-bilaterian split.
source: Eclosion hormone (EH) and bursicon originated prior to the cnidarian-bilaterian split, whereas ecdysis-triggering hormone (ETH) and crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) evolved in the bilaterian last common ancestor (LCA).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic distribution data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4A.

claim: Ecdysis-triggering hormone (ETH) and crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) evolved in the bilaterian last common ancestor (LCA).
source: Eclosion hormone (EH) and bursicon originated prior to the cnidarian-bilaterian split, whereas ecdysis-triggering hormone (ETH) and crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) evolved in the bilaterian last common ancestor (LCA).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic distribution analysis showing these components across bilaterian lineages but not in cnidarians.

claim: EH, CCAP and bursicon are present in Onychophora.
source: Identification of EH, CCAP and bursicon in Onychophora and EH, ETH and CCAP in Tardigrada suggests that the pathway was present in the panarthropod LCA.
evidence: This is based on genomic and transcriptomic screening data presented in the study.

claim: EH, ETH and CCAP are present in Tardigrada.
source: Identification of EH, CCAP and bursicon in Onychophora and EH, ETH and CCAP in Tardigrada suggests that the pathway was present in the panarthropod LCA.
evidence: This is based on genomic and transcriptomic screening data presented in the study.

claim: The ecdysis pathway was present in the panarthropod last common ancestor.
source: Identification of EH, CCAP and bursicon in Onychophora and EH, ETH and CCAP in Tardigrada suggests that the pathway was present in the panarthropod LCA.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of pathway components across panarthropod lineages.

claim: Trunk is an ancient extracellular signalling molecule and a well-established paralog of the insect peptide prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH).
source: Trunk, an ancient extracellular signalling molecule and a well-established paralog of the insect peptide prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH), is present in the non-bilaterian ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi.
evidence: This is supported by previous literature and confirmed by the current study's phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Trunk is present in the non-bilaterian ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi.
source: Trunk, an ancient extracellular signalling molecule and a well-established paralog of the insect peptide prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH), is present in the non-bilaterian ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi.
evidence: This is demonstrated through similarity searches and clustering analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ctenophore trunk peptide constitutes the first case of a ctenophore signalling peptide with homology to a neuropeptide.
source: This constitutes the first case of a ctenophore signalling peptide with homology to a neuropeptide.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on the identification of trunk in Mnemiopsis leidyi.

claim: The neuroendocrine components underlying moulting remain elusive for the majority of ecdysozoans outside of Arthropoda.
source: Despite superficial similarities of the 'moulting behaviour' within Ecdysozoa, the neuroendocrine components underlying this process remain elusive for the majority of the ecdysozoans outside of Arthropoda.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the current state of research.

claim: The gene regulatory network responsible for ecdysis in Caenorhabditis elegans remains to be fully resolved.
source: This includes well-established model organisms such as the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, for which the gene regulatory network responsible for ecdysis remains to be fully resolved (Frand et al., 2005; reviewed by Page et al., 2014 and Lažetić and Fay, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles on C. elegans moulting.

claim: In arthropods, ecdysis can be divided into three distinct stages: pre-ecdysis, ecdysis and post-ecdysis.
source: In arthropods, ecdysis can be divided into three distinct stages, pre-ecdysis, ecdysis and post-ecdysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about arthropod moulting behavior.

claim: Each stage of ecdysis correlates with major behavioural, molecular and cellular changes and encompasses a series of specific muscular contractions controlled by a cascade of hormones and neuropeptides.
source: Each of these stages correlates with major behavioural, molecular and cellular changes and encompasses a series of specific muscular contractions controlled by a cascade of hormones and neuropeptides (Truman, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Truman (2005).

claim: The major components of the peptidergic signalling pathway in insects are ecdysis-triggering hormone (ETH), eclosion hormone (EH), crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) and bursicon.
source: Studies in insects have revealed that the major components of this peptidergic signalling pathway are ecdysis-triggering hormone (ETH), eclosion hormone (EH), crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) and bursicon (Gammie and Truman, 1997a; Gammie and Truman, 1997b; Zitnan et al., 1999; Clark et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2006a; Kim et al., 2006b; Arakane et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on insect moulting.

claim: PTTH initiates a signalling cascade that results in the biosynthesis of ecdysteroids.
source: PTTH initiates a signalling cascade that results in the biosynthesis of ecdysteroids (i.e., steroid hormones synthesised from ingested cholesterol), including ecdysone (E) and 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and represents established knowledge about the insect moulting cascade.

claim: The decline of the ecdysone titre due to the ecdysone-inactivating enzyme cytochrome P450 protein Cyp18a1 triggers the release of ETH.
source: The decline of the ecdysone titre due to the ecdysone-inactivating enzyme cytochrome P450 protein Cyp18a1 (Guittard et al., 2011; reviewed by Rewitz et al., 2013) triggers the release of ETH that, in turn, causes the release of EH.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on ecdysone metabolism and its role in triggering ETH release.

claim: ETH and EH mutually enhance one another in a positive feedback loop to control and regulate pre-ecdysis behaviour.
source: These two hormones mutually enhance one another in a positive feedback loop to control and regulate pre-ecdysis behaviour (Figure 1).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and represents established knowledge about the insect moulting cascade.

claim: The release of CCAP, caused by EH, causes pre-ecdysis to cease and initiates the ecdysis motor program.
source: With the ensuing release of CCAP, caused by EH, pre-ecdysis ceases and the ecdysis motor program is initiated.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and represents established knowledge about the insect moulting cascade.

claim: Bursicon responds to increasing levels of CCAP and initiates post-ecdysis behaviour and cuticle tanning.
source: Finally, bursicon responds to the increasing levels of CCAP and initiates post-ecdysis behaviour and cuticle tanning (Figure 1).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and represents established knowledge about the insect moulting cascade.

claim: Ecdysteroids and the required genes responsible for their biosynthesis are present outside of Ecdysozoa.
source: Comparative biochemical, genomic and transcriptomic analyses revealed that ecdysteroids and the required genes responsible for their biosynthesis are present outside of Ecdysozoa, showing that some key molecular players of moulting predate the origin of Ecdysozoa (Mendis et al., 1984; Nolte et al., 1986; Garcia et al., 1989; Barker et al., 1990; Schumann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies identifying ecdysteroids in non-ecdysozoan taxa.

claim: Some key molecular players of moulting predate the origin of Ecdysozoa.
source: Comparative biochemical, genomic and transcriptomic analyses revealed that ecdysteroids and the required genes responsible for their biosynthesis are present outside of Ecdysozoa, showing that some key molecular players of moulting predate the origin of Ecdysozoa (Mendis et al., 1984; Nolte et al., 1986; Garcia et al., 1989; Barker et al., 1990; Schumann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of ecdysteroids outside Ecdysozoa, supported by citations.

claim: PTTH is believed to have evolved from the duplication of the ancient and widely distributed bilaterian signalling molecule-encoding gene trunk.
source: PTTH is a neurohormone with a proposed origin at the base of Arthropoda that is believed to have evolved from the duplication of the ancient and widely distributed bilaterian signalling molecule-encoding gene trunk (Rewitz et al., 2009; Jékely, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies proposing this evolutionary relationship.

claim: The PTTH peptide is present in Drosophila and Tribolium but absent in the house spider Parasteatoda tepidariorum and the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis.
source: By screening 39 metazoan genomes and 57 transcriptomes (Supplementary file 1), we found that the PTTH peptide is present in Drosophila and Tribolium but absent in the house spider Parasteatoda tepidariorum and the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis, suggesting that PTTH is an insect innovation (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on genomic and transcriptomic screening data presented in the study.

claim: PTTH is an insect innovation.
source: By screening 39 metazoan genomes and 57 transcriptomes (Supplementary file 1), we found that the PTTH peptide is present in Drosophila and Tribolium but absent in the house spider Parasteatoda tepidariorum and the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis, suggesting that PTTH is an insect innovation (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the restricted distribution of PTTH to insects among arthropods.

claim: The ablation of PTTH-producing neurons in Drosophila generates an imbalance in ecdysone biosynthesis, causing developmental delay, prolonged duration of feeding and larger individuals with reduced fecundity.
source: The ablation of PTTH-producing neurons in Drosophila generates an imbalance in ecdysone biosynthesis, causing developmental delay, prolonged duration of feeding and larger individuals with reduced fecundity (McBrayer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McBrayer et al. (2007).

claim: PTTH, at least in Drosophila, regulates developmental timing and body size, but is not essential for moulting.
source: These findings indicate that PTTH, at least in Drosophila, regulates developmental timing and body size, but is not essential for moulting.
evidence: This is inferred from the ablation experiments showing that flies can still moult without PTTH.

claim: Trunk has previously been identified in arthropods, annelids, mollusks and the cephalochordate Branchiostoma floridae.
source: Trunk, the paralog of ptth, has previously been identified in arthropods, annelids, mollusks and the cephalochordate Branchiostoma floridae (Jékely, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jékely (2013).

claim: The phyletic distribution of trunk extends to onychophorans, tardigrades, gastrotrichs, brachiopods, nemerteans, ectoprocts, phoronids and hemichordates.
source: Our study expands the phyletic distribution of trunk to onychophorans, tardigrades, gastrotrichs, brachiopods, nemerteans, ectoprocts, phoronids and hemichordates (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on the genomic and transcriptomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: A trunk ortholog was not found in the genome of the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis.
source: Although we did not find a trunk ortholog in the genome of the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis, our similarity searches against the NCBI protein database led to the identification of this protein in other anthozoans, namely Stylophora pistillata (PFX31008.1) and Orbicella faveolata (XP_020630744.1 and XP_020630745.1).
evidence: This is based on the absence of trunk in the N. vectensis genome but its presence in other anthozoan databases.

claim: Trunk is present in other anthozoans, namely Stylophora pistillata and Orbicella faveolata.
source: Although we did not find a trunk ortholog in the genome of the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis, our similarity searches against the NCBI protein database led to the identification of this protein in other anthozoans, namely Stylophora pistillata (PFX31008.1) and Orbicella faveolata (XP_020630744.1 and XP_020630745.1).
evidence: This is based on similarity searches against the NCBI protein database.

claim: A trunk-like peptide in the ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi has high similarity (p-value < 1e-05) to lophotrochozoan, deuterostome and ecdysozoan trunk sequences.
source: More importantly, our multi-species screen also recovered a trunk-like peptide in the ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi with high similarity (p-value < 1e-05) to lophotrochozoan, deuterostome and ecdysozoan trunk sequences (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is based on similarity searches showing statistically significant matches.

claim: Homology of the ctenophore trunk-like peptide with the insect trunk paralog, ptth, was demonstrated by similarity-based clustering.
source: By similarity-based clustering we were able to demonstrate homology of the ctenophore trunk-like peptide with the insect trunk paralog, ptth (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1; see also Rewitz et al., 2009; Jékely, 2013).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A and supported by previous studies.

claim: The phyletic distribution of trunk extends to the ctenophores.
source: This extends the phyletic distribution of trunk to the ctenophores (see, e.g., Halanych, 2004; Dunn et al., 2008; Moroz et al., 2014; Jékely et al., 2015; Pisani et al., 2015 for discussion).
evidence: This is based on the identification of trunk in Mnemiopsis leidyi and supported by citations discussing ctenophore phylogeny.

claim: PTTH and trunk share a common receptor, the tyrosine kinase torso.
source: PTTH and trunk share a common receptor, the tyrosine kinase torso (Rewitz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rewitz et al. (2009).

claim: Torso is much more ancient than commonly assumed.
source: Similar to its ligands, torso (Rewitz et al., 2009) proved also to be much more ancient than commonly assumed.
evidence: This is inferred from the broad phyletic distribution of torso found in this study.

claim: Torso sequences were identified in deuterostomes, lophotrochozoans, cnidarians and ecdysozoans.
source: We identified torso sequences in deuterostomes, lophotrochozoans, cnidarians and ecdysozoans (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the trunk-torso neuropeptide signalling pathway dates back at least as far as the last common ancestor of Cnidaria, Ctenophora and Bilateria and is thus not restricted to Bilateria as suggested previously (e.g., Jékely, 2013) (Figures 2A,B and 4A).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The trunk-torso neuropeptide signalling pathway dates back at least as far as the last common ancestor of Cnidaria, Ctenophora and Bilateria.
source: We identified torso sequences in deuterostomes, lophotrochozoans, cnidarians and ecdysozoans (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the trunk-torso neuropeptide signalling pathway dates back at least as far as the last common ancestor of Cnidaria, Ctenophora and Bilateria and is thus not restricted to Bilateria as suggested previously (e.g., Jékely, 2013) (Figures 2A,B and 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the phyletic distribution of trunk and torso across these lineages.

claim: The trunk-torso neuropeptide signalling pathway is not restricted to Bilateria.
source: We identified torso sequences in deuterostomes, lophotrochozoans, cnidarians and ecdysozoans (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the trunk-torso neuropeptide signalling pathway dates back at least as far as the last common ancestor of Cnidaria, Ctenophora and Bilateria and is thus not restricted to Bilateria as suggested previously (e.g., Jékely, 2013) (Figures 2A,B and 4A).
evidence: This contradicts previous suggestions and is based on the identification of these components in cnidarians and ctenophores.

claim: ETH was first identified as a hormone released in response to decreasing ecdysone levels in insects.
source: In insects, the first hormone released in response to decreasing ecdysone levels is usually ETH (Zitnan et al., 1996; Zitnan et al., 1999) although in the lepidopteran Manduca sexta the neuropeptide corozanin acts as the trigger for the release of ETH from the epitracheal glands (Kim et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on ETH function in insects.

claim: In the lepidopteran Manduca sexta, the neuropeptide corozanin acts as the trigger for the release of ETH from the epitracheal glands.
source: In insects, the first hormone released in response to decreasing ecdysone levels is usually ETH (Zitnan et al., 1996; Zitnan et al., 1999) although in the lepidopteran Manduca sexta the neuropeptide corozanin acts as the trigger for the release of ETH from the epitracheal glands (Kim et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim et al. (2004).

claim: Knockdown of the eth gene in Drosophila leads to lethality at the expected onset of ecdysis.
source: Knockdown of the eth gene in Drosophila (Park et al., 2002) and of eth and its receptors in Tribolium and Schistocerca (Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017) lead to lethality at the expected onset of ecdysis, demonstrating the essential role of the ETH peptidergic signalling system in moulting (Park et al., 2002; Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on ETH function.

claim: Knockdown of eth and its receptors in Tribolium and Schistocerca leads to lethality at the expected onset of ecdysis.
source: Knockdown of the eth gene in Drosophila (Park et al., 2002) and of eth and its receptors in Tribolium and Schistocerca (Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017) lead to lethality at the expected onset of ecdysis, demonstrating the essential role of the ETH peptidergic signalling system in moulting (Park et al., 2002; Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on ETH function.

claim: The ETH peptidergic signalling system plays an essential role in moulting.
source: Knockdown of the eth gene in Drosophila (Park et al., 2002) and of eth and its receptors in Tribolium and Schistocerca (Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017) lead to lethality at the expected onset of ecdysis, demonstrating the essential role of the ETH peptidergic signalling system in moulting (Park et al., 2002; Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the lethality observed when ETH is knocked down.

claim: ETH and its receptor are present in tardigrades and arthropods.
source: Our screening and phylogenetic analyses confirmed the presence of ETH and its receptor in tardigrades and arthropods, thus corroborating previous studies (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 2) (Zitnan et al., 1996; Zitnan et al., 1999; Park et al., 2002; Arakane et al., 2008; Veenstra et al., 2012; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Koziol, 2018; Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on the screening and phylogenetic analyses conducted in this study and corroborated by previous studies.

claim: The ETH ligand was only found in insects (Drosophila and Tribolium) among arthropods, but was lacking in the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis and the arachnid Parasteatoda tepidariorum.
source: For Arthropoda, the ETH ligand was only found in insects (Drosophila and Tribolium), but was lacking in the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis and the arachnid Parasteatoda tepidariorum.
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: Studies on the two mites Panonychus citri and Tetranychus urticae as well as several decapods have shown the presence of the ETH ligand in chelicerates and crustaceans.
source: However, studies on the two mites Panonychus citri and Tetranychus urticae as well as several decapods have shown the presence of the ETH ligand in chelicerates and crustaceans (in which the homology was reconfirmed by our clustering analysis) (Veenstra et al., 2012; Veenstra, 2016; Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by clustering analysis in this study.

claim: The entire ETH signalling pathway was not found in the two onychophoran genomes analysed.
source: Surprisingly, we did not find the entire ETH signalling pathway in the two onychophoran genomes analysed herein (Figures 2B and 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: Due to the fragmented nature of the onychophoran genomes, a final statement whether the ETH signalling system was indeed lost in this lineage cannot be made at present.
source: Due to the fragmented nature of the onychophoran genomes a final statement whether this signalling system was indeed lost in this lineage cannot be made at present.
evidence: This is a cautious interpretation acknowledging the limitations of the available genomic data.

claim: No eth ortholog was identified outside the panarthropods, including the nematode C. elegans.
source: No eth ortholog was identified outside the panarthropods, including the nematode C. elegans, suggesting that this gene originated in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on the absence of eth in non-panarthropod genomes screened in this study.

claim: The eth gene originated in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda.
source: No eth ortholog was identified outside the panarthropods, including the nematode C. elegans, suggesting that this gene originated in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the restriction of eth to panarthropods.

claim: The ETH receptor is present in arthropods (insects, crustaceans and arachnids), mollusks, nemerteans, brachiopods, echinoderms, cephalochordates, vertebrates and acoels.
source: Our findings on the distribution of the ETH receptor are in agreement with the results of previous studies and demonstrate the presence of this receptor in arthropods (insects, crustaceans and arachnids), mollusks, nemerteans, brachiopods, echinoderms, cephalochordates (in which we found a substantial expansion of eth-receptor homologs in the genomes of Branchiostoma floridae and B. belcheri), vertebrates and acoels (Park et al., 2003; Roller et al., 2010; Veenstra et al., 2012; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Thiel et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2019) (Figures 2B and 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis conducted in this study and corroborated by previous studies.

claim: There is a substantial expansion of eth-receptor homologs in the genomes of Branchiostoma floridae and B. belcheri.
source: Our findings on the distribution of the ETH receptor are in agreement with the results of previous studies and demonstrate the presence of this receptor in arthropods (insects, crustaceans and arachnids), mollusks, nemerteans, brachiopods, echinoderms, cephalochordates (in which we found a substantial expansion of eth-receptor homologs in the genomes of Branchiostoma floridae and B. belcheri), vertebrates and acoels (Park et al., 2003; Roller et al., 2010; Veenstra et al., 2012; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Thiel et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2019) (Figures 2B and 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Individual components of the ETH signalling system were present at the base of Bilateria.
source: This provides evidence for the presence of individual components of the ETH signalling system already at the base of Bilateria (Figures 2A and 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the broad distribution of the ETH receptor across bilaterian lineages.

claim: Eclosion hormone (EH) was first identified as a blood-borne factor in three lepidopteran species, Hyalophora cecropia, Antheraea polyphemus and Antheraea pernyi.
source: Eclosion hormone (EH) was first identified as a blood-borne factor (Truman and Riddiford, 1970) in three lepidopteran species, Hyalophora cecropia, Antheraea polyphemus and Antheraea pernyi.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original discovery of EH.

claim: A positive feedback loop between EH and ETH was found in Manduca and suggested in Tribolium.
source: A positive feedback loop between EH and ETH was found in Manduca and suggested in Tribolium (Ewer et al., 1997; Arakane et al., 2008), whereas in Drosophila, EH has been described either acting downstream of ETH (Kim et al., 2006a; Kim et al., 2006b) or in a positive endocrine feedback loop with ETH (Krüger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on EH-ETH interactions in different insect species.

claim: In Drosophila, EH has been described either acting downstream of ETH or in a positive endocrine feedback loop with ETH.
source: A positive feedback loop between EH and ETH was found in Manduca and suggested in Tribolium (Ewer et al., 1997; Arakane et al., 2008), whereas in Drosophila, EH has been described either acting downstream of ETH (Kim et al., 2006a; Kim et al., 2006b) or in a positive endocrine feedback loop with ETH (Krüger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to conflicting studies on EH function in Drosophila.

claim: eh knockout in Drosophila melanogaster did not abolish ecdysis, but instead produced flies with discrete behavioural deficits such as slow and uncoordinated eclosion.
source: Despite EH being a key regulator of ecdysis in insects, eh knockout in Drosophila melanogaster did not abolish ecdysis, but instead produced flies with discrete behavioural deficits such as slow and uncoordinated eclosion. This shows that EH is involved, but does not play an essential role, in moulting in these insects (McNabb et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McNabb et al. (1997).

claim: EH is involved, but does not play an essential role, in moulting in Drosophila.
source: Despite EH being a key regulator of ecdysis in insects, eh knockout in Drosophila melanogaster did not abolish ecdysis, but instead produced flies with discrete behavioural deficits such as slow and uncoordinated eclosion. This shows that EH is involved, but does not play an essential role, in moulting in these insects (McNabb et al., 1997).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that flies can still moult without EH, though with deficits.

claim: The result that EH is not essential for moulting in Drosophila has been contested in a more recent study using eh null mutants.
source: This result, however, has been contested in a more recent study using eh null mutants in Drosophila (Krüger et al., 2015), showing that the lack of eh function is lethal during larval fruit fly ecdysis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krüger et al. (2015) showing contradictory results.

claim: The lack of eh function is lethal during larval fruit fly ecdysis.
source: This result, however, has been contested in a more recent study using eh null mutants in Drosophila (Krüger et al., 2015), showing that the lack of eh function is lethal during larval fruit fly ecdysis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krüger et al. (2015).

claim: EH has traditionally been considered to be confined to arthropods.
source: Traditionally considered to be confined to arthropods, recent studies showed the presence of EH and its receptor, a guanylyl cyclase, in echinoderms and tardigrades (Zandawala et al., 2017; Koziol, 2018).
evidence: This represents the previous state of knowledge before recent discoveries.

claim: Recent studies showed the presence of EH and its receptor, a guanylyl cyclase, in echinoderms and tardigrades.
source: Traditionally considered to be confined to arthropods, recent studies showed the presence of EH and its receptor, a guanylyl cyclase, in echinoderms and tardigrades (Zandawala et al., 2017; Koziol, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies expanding the known distribution of EH.

claim: The EH receptor is a guanylyl cyclase.
source: Traditionally considered to be confined to arthropods, recent studies showed the presence of EH and its receptor, a guanylyl cyclase, in echinoderms and tardigrades (Zandawala et al., 2017; Koziol, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the EH receptor type.

claim: The presence of the EH ligand extends to cnidarians, acoels, hemichordates, lophotrochozoans (mollusks, annelids, nemerteans and phoronids) and onychophorans.
source: Our study corroborates these findings but considerably expands the presence of the EH ligand to cnidarians, acoels, hemichordates, lophotrochozoans (mollusks, annelids, nemerteans and phoronids) and onychophorans (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on the genomic and transcriptomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: All EH ligand orthologs harbour the six cysteine conserved residues except for Cnidaria, in which only five are present.
source: All EH ligand orthologs harbour the six cysteine conserved residues (Zitnan et al., 2007) except for Cnidaria, in which only five are present.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of EH orthologs identified in this study.

claim: The identification of the EH receptor in ambulacrarians, mollusks, annelids, nemerteans and phoronids suggests co-evolution of this ligand-receptor pair throughout Metazoa.
source: The identification of the EH receptor in ambulacrarians, mollusks, annelids, nemerteans and phoronids suggests co-evolution of this ligand-receptor pair throughout Metazoa (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlated distribution of EH ligand and receptor across metazoan lineages.

claim: The eh-receptor gene was not found in Cnidaria, Xenacoelomorpha and Onychophora.
source: Although the eh-receptor gene was not found in Cnidaria, Xenacoelomorpha and Onychophora, its distribution includes the Brachiopoda, Ectoprocta and Cephalochordata lineages.
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: The eh-receptor distribution includes the Brachiopoda, Ectoprocta and Cephalochordata lineages.
source: Although the eh-receptor gene was not found in Cnidaria, Xenacoelomorpha and Onychophora, its distribution includes the Brachiopoda, Ectoprocta and Cephalochordata lineages.
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: The ancestry of the EH peptidergic pathway dates back to the cnidarian-bilaterian split.
source: Consequently, our findings shift the ancestry of this peptidergic pathway back to the cnidarian-bilaterian split (Figures 2A and 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of EH in cnidarians and bilaterians.

claim: Crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) was first isolated from the shore crab Carcinus maenas.
source: First isolated from the shore crab Carcinus maenas, crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) is a highly conserved amidated neuropeptide that increases heart rate in crustaceans and insects (Stangier et al., 1987; Cheung et al., 1992; Lehman et al., 1993; Suggs et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original discovery and characterization of CCAP.

claim: CCAP is a highly conserved amidated neuropeptide that increases heart rate in crustaceans and insects.
source: First isolated from the shore crab Carcinus maenas, crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) is a highly conserved amidated neuropeptide that increases heart rate in crustaceans and insects (Stangier et al., 1987; Cheung et al., 1992; Lehman et al., 1993; Suggs et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on CCAP function.

claim: CCAP accelerates the frequency and amplitude of oviduct contractions in the locust Locusta migratoria.
source: CCAP has multiple functions in addition to its cardioacceleratory activity, such as accelerating the frequency and amplitude of oviduct contractions in the locust Locusta migratoria (Donini et al., 2001) and regulating the release of digestive enzymes in the cockroach Periplaneta americana (Sakai et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Donini et al. (2001).

claim: CCAP regulates the release of digestive enzymes in the cockroach Periplaneta americana.
source: CCAP has multiple functions in addition to its cardioacceleratory activity, such as accelerating the frequency and amplitude of oviduct contractions in the locust Locusta migratoria (Donini et al., 2001) and regulating the release of digestive enzymes in the cockroach Periplaneta americana (Sakai et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sakai et al. (2006).

claim: CCAP is important for ecdysis in crustaceans and insects where it initiates the stereotyped sequence of behaviours that mark the end of the pre-ecdysis stage.
source: CCAP is important for ecdysis in crustaceans and insects where it initiates the stereotyped sequence of behaviours that mark the end of the pre-ecdysis stage (Gammie and Truman, 1997a; Gammie and Truman, 1997b; Phlippen et al., 2000; Arakane et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on CCAP function in ecdysis.

claim: Transgenic Drosophila larvae lacking CCAP neurons moult normally and only exhibit a prolonged pre-ecdysis behaviour.
source: However, transgenic Drosophila larvae lacking CCAP neurons moult normally and only exhibit a prolonged pre-ecdysis behaviour (Clark et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clark et al. (2004).

claim: In the snail Lymnaea stagnalis, immunostaining revealed a dense network of CCAP-positive fibres that likely function to regulate parts of the feeding behaviour.
source: In the snail Lymnaea stagnalis (Vehovszky et al., 2005), immunostaining revealed a dense network of CCAP-positive fibres that likely function to regulate parts of the feeding behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vehovszky et al. (2005).

claim: In the oyster Saccostrea glomerata and in the cuttlefish Sepia officinalis, in vivo bioassays and immunohistochemistry suggested that the CCAP signalling pathway is involved in reproduction.
source: In the oyster Saccostrea glomerata (In et al., 2016) and in the cuttlefish Sepia officinalis (Endress et al., 2018), in vivo bioassays using synthesised neuropeptides and immunohistochemistry suggested that the CCAP signalling pathway is involved in reproduction (e.g., spawning, oocyte transport, egg-laying).
evidence: This is supported by citations to In et al. (2016) and Endress et al. (2018).

claim: Sepia CCAP has been shown to increase the tonus of the vena cava, demonstrating its role in the regulation of hemolymph circulation.
source: Additionally, Sepia CCAP has been shown to increase the tonus of the vena cava, demonstrating its role in the regulation of hemolymph circulation (Endress et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Endress et al. (2018).

claim: In both mollusks and arthropods, CCAP functions in feeding, reproduction and regulation of hemolymph circulation.
source: These results indicate that in both, mollusks and arthropods, CCAP functions in feeding, reproduction and regulation of hemolymph circulation, suggesting that these may have been its ancestral roles.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional studies in mollusks and arthropods.

claim: Feeding, reproduction and regulation of hemolymph circulation may have been the ancestral roles of CCAP.
source: These results indicate that in both, mollusks and arthropods, CCAP functions in feeding, reproduction and regulation of hemolymph circulation, suggesting that these may have been its ancestral roles.
evidence: This is speculated based on the conserved functions across mollusks and arthropods.

claim: In arthropods, co-option of CCAP into the ecdysis pathway expanded its set of functions to include moulting.
source: In arthropods, co-option of CCAP into the ecdysis pathway expanded this set of functions to include moulting.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of CCAP in the ecdysis pathway in arthropods but not in mollusks.

claim: The CCAP receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that was first described from the Drosophila genome.
source: The CCAP receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that was first described from the Drosophila genome and subsequently identified in many other insects (Cazzamali et al., 2003; Arakane et al., 2008; Vogel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying and characterizing the CCAP receptor.

claim: The CCAP receptor was subsequently identified in many other insects.
source: The CCAP receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that was first described from the Drosophila genome and subsequently identified in many other insects (Cazzamali et al., 2003; Arakane et al., 2008; Vogel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying the CCAP receptor in insects.

claim: The CCAP ligand is present in mollusks, annelids, arthropods and tardigrades.
source: We confirm here the presence of a CCAP ligand in mollusks, annelids, arthropods and tardigrades, as stated earlier (Veenstra, 2010; Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2014; Ahn et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Koziol, 2018), and extend the distribution of the CCAP ligand to three additional lophotrochozoan phyla (Nemertea, Platyhelminthes and Rotifera) as well as to the remaining panarthropod phylum Onychophora (Figures 2B and 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study and corroborated by previous studies.

claim: The distribution of the CCAP ligand extends to three additional lophotrochozoan phyla (Nemertea, Platyhelminthes and Rotifera) as well as to the remaining panarthropod phylum Onychophora.
source: We confirm here the presence of a CCAP ligand in mollusks, annelids, arthropods and tardigrades, as stated earlier (Veenstra, 2010; Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2014; Ahn et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Koziol, 2018), and extend the distribution of the CCAP ligand to three additional lophotrochozoan phyla (Nemertea, Platyhelminthes and Rotifera) as well as to the remaining panarthropod phylum Onychophora (Figures 2B and 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: The CCAP ligand is absent from all investigated deuterostome genomes.
source: Interestingly, the CCAP ligand is absent from all investigated deuterostome genomes analysed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: The ccap-receptor ortholog was found in acoels, lophotrochozoans and panarthropods except Onychophora.
source: The ccap-receptor ortholog was found in acoels, lophotrochozoans and panarthropods except Onychophora (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The CCAP receptor was found in all deuterostome phyla (Echinodermata, Hemichordata, Vertebrata, Cephalochordata) except Tunicata.
source: Surprisingly, we found the receptor also in all deuterostome phyla (Echinodermata, Hemichordata, Vertebrata, Cephalochordata) except Tunicata (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The CCAP ligand-receptor pair originated at the base of Bilateria.
source: These results reinforce the suggested origin of the ligand-receptor pair at the base of Bilateria and points towards a possible loss of the CCAP ligand in the Deuterostomia lineage (Figures 2B and 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of CCAP ligand and receptor across bilaterian lineages.

claim: There was a possible loss of the CCAP ligand in the Deuterostomia lineage.
source: These results reinforce the suggested origin of the ligand-receptor pair at the base of Bilateria and points towards a possible loss of the CCAP ligand in the Deuterostomia lineage (Figures 2B and 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of the receptor but absence of the ligand in deuterostomes.

claim: Bursicon was identified as a neurohormone responsible for cuticle sclerotization and melanisation (tanning) during post-ecdysis.
source: Bursicon was identified as a neurohormone responsible for cuticle sclerotization and melanisation (tanning) during post-ecdysis (Cottrell, 1962a; Cottrell, 1962b; Fraenkel and Hsiao, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original studies identifying bursicon function.

claim: Bursicon has a mild effect on the regulation of pre-ecdysis and is important for the proper execution of post-ecdysis in Manduca, Drosophila and Tribolium.
source: Recent studies have shown that bursicon also has a mild effect on the regulation of pre-ecdysis and is important for the proper execution of post-ecdysis in Manduca, Drosophila and Tribolium as well as for the development of wings and other integumentary structures (Baker and Truman, 2002; Dewey et al., 2004; Arakane et al., 2008; Bai and Palli, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on bursicon function in insects.

claim: Bursicon is important for the development of wings and other integumentary structures.
source: Recent studies have shown that bursicon also has a mild effect on the regulation of pre-ecdysis and is important for the proper execution of post-ecdysis in Manduca, Drosophila and Tribolium as well as for the development of wings and other integumentary structures (Baker and Truman, 2002; Dewey et al., 2004; Arakane et al., 2008; Bai and Palli, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on bursicon function in insects.

claim: Together with the ecdysis-triggering hormone signalling system, bursicon is an indispensable component of the moulting behaviour in insects.
source: Together with the ecdydis-triggering hormone signalling system, bursicon is an indispensable component of the moulting behaviour in insects (Arakane et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arakane et al. (2008).

claim: Bursicon is present outside Ecdysozoa, for example in the anthozoan Nematostella vectensis, the echinoderm Strongylocentrotus purpuratus as well as in annelids and mollusks.
source: Previous studies show that bursicon is present outside Ecdysozoa, for example in the anthozoan Nematostella vectensis, the echinoderm Strongylocentrotus purpuratus as well as in annelids and mollusks (Jékely, 2013; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2014; Ahn et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies identifying bursicon outside Ecdysozoa.

claim: The distribution of bursicon (receptor and/or ligand) extends to the hemichordate, nemertean, phoronid, rotifer and onychophoran phyla.
source: Our work confirms the presence of the complete bursicon signalling system in all arthropod genomes analysed here and extends its distribution (receptor and/or ligand) to the hemichordate, nemertean, phoronid, rotifer and onychophoran phyla (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: Bursicon and its receptor rickets are absent in tardigrades.
source: Interestingly, bursicon and its receptor rickets are absent in tardigrades, suggesting the loss of the bursicon peptidergic signalling in this lineage (Figures 2B and 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: The loss of the bursicon peptidergic signalling in tardigrades is suggested.
source: Interestingly, bursicon and its receptor rickets are absent in tardigrades, suggesting the loss of the bursicon peptidergic signalling in this lineage (Figures 2B and 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of bursicon and its receptor in tardigrades.

claim: Independent proneuropeptide and peptide prohormone surveys in tardigrade genomic and EST data also failed to detect the bursicon ligand-receptor pair in different tardigrade species.
source: The latter findings are corroborated by independent proneuropeptide and peptide prohormone surveys in the tardigrade genomic and EST data that also failed to detect this ligand-receptor pair in different tardigrade species (Christie et al., 2011; Koziol, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to independent studies corroborating the absence of bursicon in tardigrades.

claim: The bursicon receptor was not identified in any deuterostome or non-arthropod ecdysozoan lineage.
source: We did not identify the receptor in any deuterostome or non-arthropod ecdysozoan lineage (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claim: The PTTH, ETH, EH, CCAP and bursicon peptide signalling systems are lacking in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: The PTTH, ETH, EH, CCAP and bursicon peptide signalling systems are lacking in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (cf. our study and, e.g., Page et al., 2014; Lažetić and Fay, 2017; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study and corroborated by previous studies.

claim: The ecdysteroid ecdysone (E), 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), and various halloween gene products have been reported absent from the C. elegans genome.
source: Additionally, other key moulting components, such as the ecdysteroid ecdysone (E), 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), and various halloween gene products have also been reported absent from the C. elegans genome (Frand et al., 2005; Schumann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on C. elegans moulting components.

claim: An extensive body of research on moulting in C. elegans suggests an entirely different molecular machinery controlling this behaviour in this free-living nematode.
source: An extensive body of research on moulting in C. elegans suggests an entirely different molecular machinery controlling this behaviour in this free-living nematode (Russel et al., 2011; for review Lažetić and Fay, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on C. elegans moulting.

claim: E and 20E were identified in parasitic nematodes.
source: Interestingly, however, E and 20E were identified in parasitic nematodes (Cleator et al., 1987; Shea et al., 2004) and, outside Ecdysozoa, in the platyhelminth Monieza expansa, the gastropod mollusks Lymnaea stagnalis and Helix pomatia as well as in the hirudinean annelid Hirudo medicinalis (Mendis et al., 1984; Nolte et al., 1986; Garcia et al., 1989; Barker et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying ecdysteroids in parasitic nematodes.

claim: E and 20E were identified outside Ecdysozoa in the platyhelminth Monieza expansa, the gastropod mollusks Lymnaea stagnalis and Helix pomatia as well as in the hirudinean annelid Hirudo medicinalis.
source: Interestingly, however, E and 20E were identified in parasitic nematodes (Cleator et al., 1987; Shea et al., 2004) and, outside Ecdysozoa, in the platyhelminth Monieza expansa, the gastropod mollusks Lymnaea stagnalis and Helix pomatia as well as in the hirudinean annelid Hirudo medicinalis (Mendis et al., 1984; Nolte et al., 1986; Garcia et al., 1989; Barker et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying ecdysteroids in non-ecdysozoan taxa.

claim: Key peptidergic components of the arthropod ecdysis pathway emerged prior to the protostome-deuterostome split.
source: We show that key peptidergic components of the arthropod ecdysis pathway emerged prior to the protostome-deuterostome split, and thus considerably earlier than commonly assumed.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the phyletic distribution data.

claim: EH, CCAP and the bursicon signalling systems are more widespread among non-moulting animals than previously appreciated.
source: EH, CCAP and the bursicon signalling systems are more widespread among non-moulting animals than previously appreciated.
evidence: This is based on the identification of these components in non-ecdysozoan lineages.

claim: The presence of the eth-receptor ortholog in ecdysozoans, lophotrochozoans and deuterostomes, in combination with the restriction of its known ligand to insects, arachnids and tardigrades, suggests a scenario in which promiscuous ligand/receptor relationships can lead to novel signalling interactions.
source: The presence of the eth-receptor ortholog in ecdysozoans, lophotrochozoans and deuterostomes, in combination with the restriction of its known ligand to insects, arachnids and tardigrades, suggests a scenario in which promiscuous ligand/receptor relationships can lead to novel signalling interactions that provide new opportunities for natural selection to generate novel functions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is speculated based on the distribution pattern of ETH ligand and receptor.

claim: Promiscuous ligand/receptor relationships can provide new opportunities for natural selection to generate novel functions.
source: The presence of the eth-receptor ortholog in ecdysozoans, lophotrochozoans and deuterostomes, in combination with the restriction of its known ligand to insects, arachnids and tardigrades, suggests a scenario in which promiscuous ligand/receptor relationships can lead to novel signalling interactions that provide new opportunities for natural selection to generate novel functions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a general evolutionary principle applied to the ETH system.

claim: The identification of the near complete suite of the peptidergic arthropod ecdysis pathway components in Onychophora and Tardigrada strongly suggests that the entire pathway was at least functional in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda.
source: The identification of the near complete suite of the peptidergic arthropod ecdysis pathway components in Onychophora and Tardigrada strongly suggests that the entire pathway was at least functional in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda and maybe as early as in the ur-ecdysozoan (Figures 2B and 4B).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of most pathway components in onychophorans and tardigrades.

claim: The entire ecdysis pathway may have been functional as early as in the ur-ecdysozoan.
source: The identification of the near complete suite of the peptidergic arthropod ecdysis pathway components in Onychophora and Tardigrada strongly suggests that the entire pathway was at least functional in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda and maybe as early as in the ur-ecdysozoan (Figures 2B and 4B).
evidence: This is speculated based on the distribution of pathway components across ecdysozoan lineages.

claim: ETH was apparently secondarily lost in Onychophora.
source: However, considering the crucial role of the ETH and bursicon signalling systems in insect moulting, together with the apparent secondary loss of ETH in Onychophora and bursicon in Tardigrada (Figure 4B), the consequences of harbouring only the partial set of the ecdysis signalling genes should be the focus of future assessments.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of ETH in onychophoran genomes despite its presence in other panarthropods.

claim: Bursicon was apparently secondarily lost in Tardigrada.
source: However, considering the crucial role of the ETH and bursicon signalling systems in insect moulting, together with the apparent secondary loss of ETH in Onychophora and bursicon in Tardigrada (Figure 4B), the consequences of harbouring only the partial set of the ecdysis signalling genes should be the focus of future assessments.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of bursicon in tardigrade genomes despite its presence in other panarthropods.

claim: Independent recruitment of novel peptidergic components into insect ecdysis has been shown.
source: Independent recruitment of novel peptidergic components into insect ecdysis has been shown (cf. Kim et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2006a; Kim et al., 2006b; extensively reviewed by Zitnan et al., 1996), illustrating the evolutionary plasticity of this signalling pathway and calling for more detailed functional investigations into the role of individual components during moulting of the various ecdysozoan lineages.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing recruitment of new components.

claim: The ecdysis signalling pathway exhibits evolutionary plasticity.
source: Independent recruitment of novel peptidergic components into insect ecdysis has been shown (cf. Kim et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2006a; Kim et al., 2006b; extensively reviewed by Zitnan et al., 1996), illustrating the evolutionary plasticity of this signalling pathway and calling for more detailed functional investigations into the role of individual components during moulting of the various ecdysozoan lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from the independent recruitment of novel components.

claim: 39 metazoan genomes and 57 transcriptomes were screened in this study.
source: By screening 39 metazoan genomes and 57 transcriptomes (Supplementary file 1), we found that the PTTH peptide is present in Drosophila and Tribolium but absent in the house spider Parasteatoda tepidariorum and the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis, suggesting that PTTH is an insect innovation (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the scope of the genomic and transcriptomic data analyzed.
